title: Replicating the short student videos with a delayed follow-up and a behavioural outcome
why: Addresses power and measurement. It concentrates the sample on the two best-supported arms plus the peer-review video, tests them against control in a confirmatory design, and adds a delayed and a behavioural outcome.

power_target.basis: Observed effect of about 0.063 (SE 0.025 at n=853-921). The power table was empty, so the sample size is a back-of-envelope estimate of about 1,000 per arm for 80% power at 0.063. 4,000 per arm gives headroom to detect effects of about half that size and for attrition in the delayed wave.

rationale: In the source study, Science through the day (about 0.06, SE 0.025) and Science in everyday life (0.063, SE 0.025) were near the threshold among 32 uncorrected tests. The peer-review video had 0.064 (p=0.034). Only immediate trust was measured, so durability and behavioural carry-over are unknown. This confirmatory test concentrates the sample on those three videos plus control and adds a 7-day and a behavioural outcome.
contribution: Provides a Holm-corrected confirmatory test of whether short science videos raise trust, whether any effect lasts 7 days, and whether it changes a behavioural choice.
hypothesis: Each video raises immediate trust relative to control (position a). Under position b, contrasts are near zero after Holm correction. Effects at 7 days are smaller than or equal to immediate effects.
primary_outcome: Immediate post-treatment trust in science (mean of 6 items, items 4-6 reverse-coded), with 7-day trust and the behavioural choice as secondary outcomes.
comparison: Each of the three videos against control, with Holm correction across the three contrasts, covariate-adjusted for pre-treatment trust.
unresolved: Video files and hosting must be supplied by the research team.
IRB number, compensation and bonus funding are to be set by the research team.
label: Design advance

title: Does partisanship moderate the student-video effect?
why: Addresses the missing moderator and the sample. The exploratory interaction of 0.165 in the Science in everyday life arm is untested confirmatory, and partisan effects bear on where the result holds.

power_target.basis: Exploratory interaction estimate of 0.165 with SE 0.057 (E2). Interactions need roughly four times the main-effect sample, and the effect is probably inflated, so the target is set for 0.1.

rationale: In the source study, the student video 'Science in everyday life' raised trust by 0.063 (SE 0.025, p=0.012), and an exploratory arm-by-Republican interaction of 0.165 (SE 0.057) was found but never confirmed. All data came from Lucid, so we do not know whether the effect holds for Republicans or on another panel.
contribution: Provides a confirmatory, quota-sampled test of whether a short student science video raises trust more among Republicans, replicated across two panels.
hypothesis: The video raises trust more among Republican-leaning respondents than among non-Republicans (positive interaction). Under the null (position b) the interaction and the main effect are near zero.
primary_outcome: Trust in science: mean of the 6 post-treatment items, items 4-6 reverse-coded.
comparison: Arm (video vs control) by Republican identification interaction on post-treatment trust, controlling for pre-trust and panel; secondary: effect within each party group and each panel.
unresolved: The student video file must be supplied by the research team.
The second panel provider, compensation and IRB number are to be decided by the research team.
The exact wording of the six trust items should be copied from the source instrument.
label: Generalizability

title: Format versus content: separating persuasion from salience
why: Addresses design confounding. It tests whether the small gains reflect content or merely an attention cue, which discriminates between the brief-messages-work and beliefs-resist positions.

power_target.basis: Observed effect of 0.063 with SE about 0.025 at n of about 900. Detecting this at 80% power needs about 1,000 per cell.

rationale: In the source study, the 29-second student video 'Science in everyday life' raised trust by 0.063 (SE 0.025, p=0.012), but it differs from other arms in format, length and content, and 32 uncorrected tests were run. A 2x2 of content by format with a pure control tests whether such small gains come from the science framing or from an attention cue.
contribution: Separates content from format and salience in a brief trust-in-science message, which discriminates between the brief-messages-work and beliefs-resist positions.
hypothesis: If content drives the effect (position a), only the two science-framing cells raise trust relative to control and neutral cells. If salience or format alone drives it, neutral cells also move trust. If beliefs resist (position b), all contrasts are near zero.
primary_outcome: Post-treatment trust in science (mean of the 6 items, items 4-6 reverse-coded), adjusted for pre-trust.
comparison: Main effect of content (science vs neutral), main effect of format (video vs text), their interaction, and each cell vs pure control, with Holm correction.
unresolved: The actual video files and final text wording must be produced by the research team.
IRB approval number and compensation amount.
label: Theoretical debate
